account: Thornton, Morris, and colleagues compared ecological occupancy models derived from automated SpeciesNet identifications with models derived from expert identifications. Dan Morris, a developer at Google, coauthored the study. The study used 638 cameras in Washington, 263 in Montana, and 326 in Guatemala. Montana's expert workflow already used MegaDetector for initial sorting. MegaDetector 5a located animals, and SpeciesNet classified the crops, with regional species lists, taxonomic adjustments, and sequence processing. Across six AI configurations, mean absolute differences in occupancy probabilities were 0.04-0.05 in Washington, 0.05-0.07 in Montana, and 0.03-0.06 in Guatemala. These comparisons cover species present in both datasets. They do not measure the accuracy of labels on individual images. Some individual species differed substantially, with a maximum difference of 0.40 in Montana. All 94 mountain-goat detections in Montana were classified as domestic goats and omitted from the AI occupancy models. The authors report broadly similar results for shared species. The authors recommend human review for some research tasks. The study does not measure net labor savings, changed management decisions or wildlife outcomes. The author summary was first dated 17 March 2026, and the full paper appeared on 6 May 2026. On 10 October 2026 Michael Tabak, an ecologist who is not affiliated with Google or the study team, posted a preprint that tested a SpeciesNet-based workflow on 63 cameras in Malawi. People reviewed 5 percent of the images, and a retrained project model labeled the rest. Occupancy estimates differed from a full human review by 0.11 on average. No cited source reports that a monitoring program adopted the fully automated workflow by October 2026.

segment: Ecological occupancy modeling from camera images
summary: Models built from MegaDetector and SpeciesNet labels came close to expert-based models, with mean occupancy differences of 0.03-0.07 across study areas; some species were missed or misclassified.
taxonomy_note: The observed result is useful ecological modeling with automated species identifications. Faster research and conservation improvements are not measured outcomes in this study.
title: Occupancy models built from SpeciesNet identifications come close to expert-based models for most shared species and miss some species
unrated_because: The study is a retrospective comparison on images that experts had already labeled, and no source reports that any team adopted the automated workflow or saved labor with it.
